name: Cyproterone acetate

lead: Cyproterone acetate is a prescription hormone drug that blocks androgens. Doctors use it, often with an estrogen pill, in women for excess hair growth, severe acne and androgen-related hair loss, giving calmer follicles and oil glands, clearer skin and less thinning.

It blocks androgen receptors and, as a progestin, lowers the brain signals that drive testosterone production in men and estradiol in women. A Dutch review described spironolactone or cyproterone acetate with an oral contraceptive as the safest and most effective approach for hirsutism in women with PCOS or idiopathic hirsutism. Use for appearance in men is mostly anecdotal and rarely discussed in forums.

paras: It is prescribed by a doctor, most often combined with an estrogen-containing pill for women with hyperandrogenism. Hair and skin changes build over months, and treatment is reviewed periodically.

Reported risks include meningioma at higher cumulative doses, liver toxicity, and clotting risk when combined with estrogen pills. Regulators restrict long-term high-dose use in many regions. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Cyproterone acetate blocks androgens and lowers hormone production, calming follicles and oil glands for less thinning, hirsutism and acne. It is established clinical practice for women with hyperandrogenism; appearance use in men is mostly anecdotal.

lead: Cyproterone acetate (CPA) is a synthetic steroidal antiandrogen and progestin. It blocks androgen receptors and, through its progestogenic action, suppresses gonadotropin release and so lowers testosterone production in men and estradiol in women [1][2]. It is used for palliation in advanced prostate cancer, for hirsutism and severe acne in women (often with ethinylestradiol), and to reduce sexual drive in men with paraphilias [1].

In hair and appearance contexts, CPA is relevant to female pattern hair loss and hirsutism. A Dutch review described spironolactone or cyproterone acetate combined with an oral contraceptive as the safest and most effective approach for hirsutism in women with PCOS or idiopathic hirsutism [3]. Its use is limited in many regions by a dose-dependent risk of meningioma and liver toxicity reported in a general reference [1].
Sources for this entry contain very little community discussion; mentions on T Nation are brief [4][5].
infobox: Hirsutism, acne, advanced prostate cancer, paraphilia treatment [1]

paras: CPA is used in advanced prostate cancer as a palliative agent and for reducing hypersexuality or paraphilic behaviour in men [1]. Early trials compared it with other agents in oncology, including a 1989 randomised trial with tamoxifen in pancreatic carcinoma, and a 1990 multicentre trial and review covered clinical applications of antiandrogens [6][7][8].

In women, CPA is prescribed for hirsutism, severe acne, seborrhea and androgenetic alopecia associated with PCOS or androgen excess, most often at a low dose combined with ethinylestradiol in a 21 on, 7 off regimen [1]. Reviews of androgenetic alopecia describe hormonal investigation in women with signs of hyperandrogenism to direct therapy [9]. A 2003 randomised trial compared treatments for hyperandrogenic alopecia in women, and a 2016 Cochrane review assessed randomised trials of interventions for female pattern hair loss [10][11].

A 1987 comparative clinical study examined antiandrogens in hirsutism, and the Dutch review recommends CPA or spironolactone with an oral contraceptive for hirsutism [3][12]. For the combined pill, a 2024 randomised trial in overweight women with PCOS compared CPA with ethinylestradiol plus metformin against liraglutide plus metformin over 12 weeks; both improved menstrual cycle and some hormonal and glycaemic measures [13]. Evidence for scalp hair loss specifically rests on the trials and reviews above [10][11].

A general reference reports a substantially elevated incidence of meningioma, with hazard ratios above 20 for cumulative exposures over 30 grams, and hepatotoxicity, leading regulators to contraindicate it in patients with prior meningioma and to advise avoiding doses above 10 mg daily for extended periods [1]. Combined oral contraceptives are associated with venous thrombosis, and a Cochrane network meta-analysis compared the thrombosis risk across pill types [14].

CPA competitively blocks androgen receptors and activates progesterone receptors, which suppresses GnRH pulsatility and reduces LH and FSH; in men testosterone is reduced by up to 70 to 90 percent at standard doses according to a general reference [1]. CPA is classed among 17-alpha-hydroxyprogesterone derivatives in progestin classifications [2]. Its progestogenic effect contributes to ovulation inhibition when combined with ethinylestradiol [1].

On T Nation, CPA appears incidentally: a 2023 poster argued in a discussion of estradiol and libido that one could take CPA to suppress remaining testosterone, and a 2019 thread on post-isotretinoin recovery quotes a review of progestogens with antiandrogenic properties that includes cyproterone acetate [4][5]. No looksmax.org threads on CPA were found.

Human research includes a 2003 randomised trial in hyperandrogenic alopecia in women, a Cochrane review of female pattern hair loss, a 1987 comparative study in hirsutism, a 2024 PCOS randomised trial, and a 1989 randomised trial in pancreatic carcinoma [7][10][11][12][13]. No studies of CPA in male pattern hair loss were identified.
